summary: A quick thinking-style quiz about patterns, logic, creativity, focus, communication, and problem-solving instincts.

landing.quickStartText: Choose the answer that feels most like how your mind works. Your result appears instantly at the end.

footer.aboutText: This Intelligence Spectrum Quiz is designed for entertainment and self-reflection. It is not an IQ test, psychological assessment, clinical tool, school exam, employment test, or official measure of intelligence. Results describe broad thinking styles and problem-solving preferences, not fixed ability, talent, or future performance. The questions are simplified personality-style prompts meant to be fun, quick, and easy to share.

profiles.title: Your strongest thinking style is Pattern Thinker.
profiles.copy: You notice repeats, links, and hidden structure quickly. Your mind style is strongest when a problem has signals that can be compared.

profiles.title: Your strongest thinking style is Creative Strategist.
profiles.copy: You like fresh angles, flexible plans, and useful ideas that others may miss. Your problem-solving style works best when there is room to imagine options.

profiles.title: Your strongest thinking style is Practical Solver.
profiles.copy: You look for the step that works in real life. Your thinking style is grounded, clear, and focused on useful progress.

profiles.title: Your strongest thinking style is Deep Analyst.
profiles.copy: You prefer to understand the reason behind a result. Your mind style is careful, exact, and comfortable with deeper questions.

profiles.title: Your strongest thinking style is Instinctive Solver.
profiles.copy: You trust fast signals and learn by testing ideas in motion. Your problem-solving style is quick, responsive, and energetic.

profiles.title: Your strongest thinking style is Verbal Connector.
profiles.copy: You make sense of problems through clear words, examples, and shared meaning. Your thinking style gets sharper when ideas are explained well.

profiles.title: Your strongest thinking style is Visual Reasoner.
profiles.copy: You think well through shapes, spaces, layouts, and mental pictures. Your mind style is strong when information can be seen or arranged.

profiles.title: Your strongest thinking style is Systems Thinker.
profiles.copy: You notice how parts affect each other. Your problem-solving style is strongest when you can map the whole system before choosing a move.

stageGroups.title: First Thinking Instincts
stageGroups.encouragement: Good start. Your first instincts are already shaping the result.

questions.prompt: When a problem appears suddenly, what do you usually notice first?
choices: The pattern that seems to repeat
The part that needs a practical step
questions.explanation: Your first focus often reveals your natural thinking style.

questions.prompt: What makes you feel ready to solve something new?
questions.explanation: Different minds prepare through structure, action, or language.

questions.prompt: How do you usually begin when the answer is not obvious?
questions.explanation: This shows the entry point your mind prefers.

questions.prompt: A puzzle has too much information. What feels most natural?
questions.explanation: Sorting, action, and cause-effect thinking are all valid paths.

questions.prompt: Which kind of clue feels easiest for you to use?
questions.explanation: Your preferred clue format points toward your thinking profile.

questions.prompt: If two answers both seem possible, what helps you choose?
choices: Look for the most original option
questions.explanation: Choice pressure often reveals how you organize uncertainty.

stageGroups.title: Pattern And Detail
stageGroups.encouragement: Nice. Now the quiz starts testing how you handle signals and small details.

questions.prompt: When a sequence changes, what do you check first?
choices: What repeats before and after the change
questions.explanation: A changing sequence can be read through repeats, action, or meaning.

questions.prompt: A set of symbols looks almost the same. What helps you compare them?
choices: Hold the shapes in your mind
Check one feature at a time
questions.explanation: Careful comparison can be visual, exact, or relationship-based.

questions.prompt: What do you trust most when spotting a hidden rule?
choices: A map of all the parts
questions.explanation: Hidden rules can stand out through structure, speed, or systems.

questions.prompt: If a detail feels out of place, what do you do first?
choices: Ask why it does not fit
questions.explanation: A strange detail can invite analysis, visual testing, or simplicity.

questions.prompt: How do you usually remember a small detail?
choices: Link it to a wider pattern
questions.explanation: Memory often follows the format that feels clearest to you.

questions.prompt: When a pattern has one missing piece, what feels most useful?
choices: Check how the whole set balances
questions.explanation: Prediction, testing, and balance each reveal a different mind style.

stageGroups.title: Problem Solving Style
stageGroups.encouragement: Good momentum. This round looks at how you move from confusion to progress.

questions.prompt: If a task feels messy, what approach feels most like you?
choices: Try a new path around it
questions.explanation: Messy tasks often reveal whether you prefer steps, reasons, or new paths.

questions.prompt: What helps you stay interested in a hard problem?
questions.explanation: Interest can come from depth, motion, or possibility.

questions.prompt: When instructions feel unclear, what do you prefer?
questions.explanation: Your preferred support shows how your mind builds clarity.

questions.prompt: How do you usually test whether an idea works?
choices: Use it on a simple case
See how it affects the wider plan
questions.explanation: Testing can be practical, logical, or system-wide.

questions.prompt: What kind of solution feels most satisfying?
choices: One that is elegant and unexpected
One that is clear and useful
questions.explanation: Satisfaction often comes from the style of solution you value most.

questions.prompt: If a first attempt fails, what feels most natural next?
choices: Try again with a faster example
Explain the issue in simpler words
questions.explanation: Recovery can come from creativity, motion, or clearer language.

stageGroups.title: Memory And Focus
stageGroups.encouragement: You are halfway into the thinking engine now. This round checks focus style without turning it into a test.

questions.prompt: How do you keep track of several small facts?
choices: Say the key words to yourself
questions.explanation: Focus can be supported by grouping, location, or language.

questions.prompt: What helps you return to a task after a break?
choices: A map of the whole task
questions.explanation: Returning to focus can depend on action, overview, or purpose.

questions.prompt: When you need to remember an idea, what sticks best?
questions.explanation: Memory becomes easier when it matches your natural format.

questions.prompt: If your attention starts drifting, what pulls it back?
questions.explanation: Some minds refocus through action, curiosity, or visual order.

questions.prompt: What kind of detail do you notice without trying?
choices: A missing piece in the logic
A part that affects the whole
questions.explanation: Automatic attention often points to your strongest thinking habit.

questions.prompt: When information is presented quickly, what do you do?
choices: Ask for the meaning in plain words
questions.explanation: Fast information can be handled through action, instinct, or clarity.

stageGroups.title: Creative Logic
stageGroups.encouragement: This is where logic and imagination start working together.

questions.prompt: What makes a new idea feel promising to you?
choices: It fits a pattern you recognize
questions.explanation: Promising ideas can feel useful, open, or patterned.

questions.prompt: When you imagine an answer, what comes first?
questions.explanation: Imagination can begin as shape, reason, or language.

questions.prompt: If a common solution feels too plain, what do you try?
questions.explanation: Improvement can come from originality, speed, or structure.

questions.prompt: What kind of connection do you enjoy finding?
choices: Two parts that affect each other
Two words that clarify the same idea
questions.explanation: Connections can be patterned, system-based, or meaning-based.

questions.prompt: How do you usually handle a blank page?
choices: Start with the first useful step
questions.explanation: Starting style can reveal how your mind turns emptiness into progress.

questions.prompt: What makes a clever answer feel complete?
choices: It changes how you see the problem
questions.explanation: Completion can mean explanation, usefulness, or a changed view.

stageGroups.title: Communication And Meaning
stageGroups.encouragement: Strong thinking is not only private. This round looks at how ideas become clear.

questions.prompt: When explaining a complex idea, what do you reach for first?
questions.explanation: Explanation style often mirrors thinking style.

questions.prompt: What makes another person's explanation easy to follow?
questions.explanation: You may prefer reasons, connections, or examples.

questions.prompt: If a message feels unclear, what do you want most?
questions.explanation: Clarity can arrive through words, layout, or action.

questions.prompt: How do you usually make a group idea better?
questions.explanation: Group thinking can improve through links, options, or organization.

questions.prompt: What kind of question do you ask most often?
choices: What happens if we change this?
questions.explanation: Questions reveal whether you seek meaning, effects, or motion.

questions.prompt: When a discussion has many opinions, what helps you think?
questions.explanation: Complex discussion can be sorted through evidence, pattern, or action.

stageGroups.title: Visual Reasoning
stageGroups.encouragement: Now the quiz shifts toward space, layout, and mental pictures.

questions.prompt: When reading a map-like layout, what do you notice first?
questions.explanation: Layout thinking can focus on path, repeats, or connections.

questions.prompt: If an object is turned around, what helps you understand it?
choices: Compare it with a known shape
questions.explanation: Mental rotation, naming, and comparison are different strengths.

questions.prompt: What kind of note would help you solve a spatial puzzle?
questions.explanation: Spatial puzzles can be supported by drawing, rules, or testing.

questions.prompt: How do you arrange information when you want it to make sense?
choices: Put it in a useful order
Show how each part affects another
questions.explanation: Arrangement can follow groups, order, or relationships.

questions.prompt: What makes a chart or diagram useful to you?
choices: It shows the whole shape quickly
questions.explanation: A useful diagram can support seeing, imagining, or explaining.

questions.prompt: If a layout feels confusing, what do you change first?
questions.explanation: Confusing layouts can be improved visually, practically, or logically.

stageGroups.title: Decision Under Pressure
stageGroups.encouragement: This round keeps the choices fair, but the timing instinct gets sharper.

questions.prompt: When time feels limited, what do you rely on most?
choices: The structure that avoids bigger problems
questions.explanation: Pressure can bring out usefulness, instinct, or system awareness.

questions.prompt: If you must choose before you know everything, what helps?
questions.explanation: Limited information can be handled through testing, pattern, or clarity.

questions.prompt: What do you do when a choice has trade-offs?
choices: Choose the step with least waste
questions.explanation: Trade-offs invite analysis, invention, or efficiency.

questions.prompt: How do you avoid overthinking a simple choice?
questions.explanation: Simple choices can be handled by use, instinct, or rules.

questions.prompt: What helps you stay calm when information changes?
questions.explanation: Change can feel manageable through pattern, planning, or explanation.

questions.prompt: When a quick decision surprises people, what is usually behind it?
choices: A fast read of the situation
A visual sense of the outcome
A creative leap that connects things
questions.explanation: Fast choices can come from instinct, visualization, or creative connection.

stageGroups.title: Systems And Strategy
stageGroups.encouragement: Strong finish building. This round looks at planning, connections, and long-view thinking.

questions.prompt: When a plan has many moving parts, what do you check first?
choices: How each part affects the others
questions.explanation: Complex plans can be approached through systems, action, or pattern risk.

questions.prompt: What makes a strategy feel strong to you?
questions.explanation: A strong strategy may feel logical, flexible, or clear.

questions.prompt: If one part of a plan changes, what do you think about next?
choices: What the next useful move is
questions.explanation: A change can invite system thinking, new options, or action.

questions.prompt: How do you usually find weak spots in a plan?
questions.explanation: Weak spots can show up through logic, visualization, or testing.

questions.prompt: What kind of long-term problem interests you most?
choices: One that needs a bold idea
questions.explanation: Long-term interest often follows your preferred problem shape.

questions.prompt: When you improve a process, what is your usual goal?
choices: Make the steps easier to use
Make the idea clearer to people
questions.explanation: Improvement can mean better flow, easier action, or clearer meaning.

questions.prompt: At the end of a hard problem, what do you enjoy most?
questions.explanation: Your final satisfaction points toward your strongest thinking style.

questions.prompt: What do people often ask you to help with?
choices: Making sense of a confusing idea
Choosing quickly when things move fast
questions.explanation: The help people seek from you often reflects a visible strength.

questions.prompt: Which final clue feels most like your mind?
questions.explanation: This final clue points to the format your mind returns to.

questions.prompt: How do you prefer your result to describe you?
questions.explanation: The words you choose reveal the thinking style you recognize in yourself.

questions.prompt: What kind of challenge would you choose next?
questions.explanation: The challenge you choose often matches the thinking style you enjoy using.

questions.prompt: Which answer feels most like your problem-solving style overall?
questions.explanation: Your final choice helps complete the thinking-style result.
